questions.q: Ask the user for one word. Display [word] four times, one on each of four lines.

teach.say: for i in range(3): repeats the indented lines three times, because range(3) counts 0, 1, 2.

brief: Ask the user for one word.
questions.starter: # Read the word, then print it four times

tests.why: Four lines exactly. Five means range(5): range(4) already gives four turns, counting 0, 1, 2, 3.
The word is read from the user, so a program with the word typed into it will fail here.
A one letter word is still printed four times.

questions.fb: range(4) counts 0, 1, 2, 3, which is four numbers, so the loop body runs four times without ever reaching 4.

questions.q: Ask the user for a word and then a whole number. Display start, then [word] on that many lines.

teach.say: range() can use a number read from the user, once int() has made it a whole number. A line before the loop is not indented, so it runs once.
code: n = int(input("How many? "))   # the user types 2

brief: The user types in two lines: a word, then a whole number.
questions.starter: # Read a word and a count, print start, then repeat the word

tests.why: start is printed once, before the loop, so it must not be indented inside it.
A count of 1 means one line. Two means the loop ran to n + 1.
range(0) runs no turns at all, so only start is printed. A line of hum here means the loop always runs once.
The count comes from input(), so it needs int() before range() can use it.

questions.fb: range(n) uses whatever number is in n, including 0, which simply means the body never runs.

questions.q: Ask the user for how many lanes there are. Display the lane numbers from 1 up to and including that number, one on each line.

teach.say: range stops before its second number, so range(1, 4) counts 1, 2, 3. To finish on n you write range(1, n + 1).

brief: The user types in one whole number: how many lanes there are.
questions.starter: # Read how many lanes there are, then number them from 1

tests.why: Starts at 1 and includes 5. A list starting at 0 means range(n) was used instead of range(1, n + 1).
One lane gives one line. Nothing at all means range(1, n) stopped before it started.
The last number must appear. A missing 3 is the off by one that range(1, n) always causes.

questions.fb: range stops before its second number, so to finish on n you write range(1, n + 1).

questions.q: Ask the user for the largest side length. For every side from 1 up to and including that number, display a line in the form [side] [side times itself].

teach.say: The counter is an ordinary number, so you can calculate with it inside the loop. Two values in one print() come out with a space between them.

brief: The user types in one whole number: the largest side length.
questions.starter: # Read the largest side, then print each side and its area

tests.why: The counter is used twice on each line: once on its own and once multiplied by itself.
A side of 1 has an area of 1, so the two numbers match here.
Every line uses its own counter value. Lines that all show the same number mean n was printed rather than i.
Two lines only. A third means the range went one too far.

questions.fb: The loop variable is an ordinary number, so you can calculate with it inside the loop.

questions.q: Ask the user for the first row number and then the last row number. Display every row number from the first to the last, both included, one on each line.

teach.say: range takes a start and a stop, and the stop is never reached, so add 1 to the last value you want.

brief: The user types in two lines: the first row number, then the last row number.
questions.starter: # Read the first and last row numbers, then list every row

tests.why: Both ends are included. A missing 7 means range(first, last).
The first and last row are the same, so exactly one line prints. Nothing means the range was empty.
The start comes from the input. A list beginning at 0 or 1 means the first number was ignored.
Four lines. Five means 1 was added to the start as well as the end.

questions.fb: range takes a start and a stop, and the stop is never reached, so the last value you want is last + 1.

questions.q: Ask the user for a whole number. Display every number from it down to 1, one on each line.

teach.say: range takes a third number, the step. A step of -1 counts down, and the stop is still never reached.

brief: The user types in one whole number.
questions.starter: # Read a number, then count down from it to 1

tests.why: Counts down and stops at 1. Nothing printed means the range still goes upwards: the third number has to be negative.
One line only. Nothing at all means the stop was 1 rather than 0, so the last value was cut off.
A 0 on the end means the stop was -1. The stop is never reached, so 0 stops the count at 1.
Two lines, counting down. Lines in the other order mean the start and stop are swapped.

questions.fb: range(start, stop, step) counts by the step, and a negative step counts down. The stop is still never reached.

questions.q: Ask the user for how many amounts there are, then for that many whole numbers. Add up the amounts and display [total] and nothing else.

teach.say: A running total is set to 0 before the loop, added to inside the loop, and printed after it.

brief: Then the user types in that many whole numbers, one on each line.
questions.starter: # Read how many amounts there are, add them up, print the total

tests.why: The total starts at 0 and grows on every turn of the loop.
One amount. A 0 means the total was printed before the loop had added anything.
A refund is negative, so write total = total + amount rather than only adding the large ones.
Two zeros total 0, and that single line still has to be printed.
The loop runs exactly as many times as the first number says, and only the total is printed.

questions.fb: A running total needs three things: set it to 0 before the loop, add to it inside the loop, print it after the loop.

questions.q: Ask the user for how many readings there are, then for that many whole numbers. Display [total], then [how many of the readings are below 0] on the next line.

teach.say: Each thing you are tracking needs its own variable, set up before the loop and updated inside it.

brief: Then the user types in that many whole numbers, one on each line.
questions.starter: # Read the readings, then print the total and the frosty count

tests.why: One reading is below 0, and the total keeps all four.
Every reading is below 0, so the count is 3 and the total is negative.
One reading, nothing below 0, and the count still has to be printed as 0.
Exactly 0 is not below 0, so the count stays at 0. This is where < and <= get mixed up.
A repeated value is counted every time it appears in the total, but only the -3 is below 0.

questions.fb: Keep a separate variable for each thing you are tracking, and update them all inside the same loop.

questions.q: Ask the user for the number of rows and then the number of stars in each row. Display one line for each row, made of that many * characters and nothing else.

teach.say: The outer loop counts the rows and the inner loop builds one row. Build the row up as a string, then print it once the inner loop has finished.

brief: The user types in two lines: the number of rows, then the number of stars in each row.
questions.starter: # Read the rows and the width, then draw the rectangle

tests.why: Three rows of four stars. One line of twelve means the print is inside the inner loop.
The smallest rectangle is one star. Nothing printed means a range that never runs.
The rows and the width are different numbers, so check they are not swapped.
More rows than stars per row. Two rows of four means the inputs are the wrong way round.

questions.fb: The outer loop counts the rows and the inner loop builds one row, which is printed once the inner loop has finished.

questions.q: Ask the user for the size of the square. Display one line for each row from 1 up to that size: the row number times 1, times 2, and so on up to the size.

teach.say: The outer counter stays still while the inner one runs all the way through, so the value you print is the two counters multiplied.

brief: Put a single space between the numbers on a line.
questions.starter: # Read the size, then print the multiplication square

tests.why: Both loops run from 1, not 0. A row of zeros means one of them started at 0.
A size of 1 gives one line holding 1 times 1.
Four lines of four numbers. Three lines means both ranges needed n + 1.
The row number stays still while the inner loop runs, so the outer counter is used in the multiplication too.

questions.fb: The outer counter stays still while the inner one runs all the way through.

questions.q: Ask the user for how many amounts there are, then for that many whole numbers. After each one display a line in the form [amount] [total so far]. At the end display [average] rounded to 1 decimal place.

teach.say: Printing inside the loop shows the total so far, while anything printed after the loop uses the finished total.

brief: The user types in a whole number: how many amounts follow, then that many whole numbers, one on each line.
questions.starter: # Read the amounts, print each with the running total, then the average

tests.why: The total so far is printed on every turn, and the average is worked out once at the end.
One amount is its own total and its own average, and / always gives a real number, so 7.0 and not 7.
A negative amount brings the total down. If the last line is a long row of decimals, the round() is missing.
Two zeros, so every line is 0 and the average is 0.0. Dividing by the count, not by 2, is what makes it work for any number of amounts.
Five amounts, five lines, then the average. A sixth line of a single number means the total was printed as well.

questions.fb: The total so far belongs inside the loop and the average after it, worked out from the finished total and how many there were.
